L1@P0: The pasch configuration and Steiner triple
L2@P0: systems
L3@P0: Masood Aryapoor∗
L4@P0: 1 Introduction
L5@P0: A Steiner triple system of order n (or ST S(n)) is a pair (X, S) where X,
L6@P0: called the foundation, is a finite set with n elements and S is a subset of P3(X)
L7@P0: (the set of all 3-subsets of X) whose elements are called blocks, such that for
L8@P0: every pair of distinct elements of X there is exactly one block in S which contains
L9@P0: both of them. It is known that an ST S(n) exists iff n ≡ 1, 3 mod 6. Such values
L10@P0: of n are called admissible. For a detailed study of them and related objects see
L11@P0: [2].
L12@P0: Another useful way to represent Steiner triple systems is to use the notion
L13@P0: of Steiner quasi-groups. A Steiner quasi-group structure on X is a binary
L14@P0: operation ⋆ on X subject to the following conditions: for every a, b ∈ X, we have
L15@P0: a ⋆ a = a, a ⋆ b = b ⋆ a, and a ⋆ (a ⋆ b) = b. It is known that there is a one-to-one
L16@P0: correspondence between Steiner triple systems with foundation X and Steiner
L17@P0: quasi-group structures on X. The correspondence is given by sending a Steiner
L18@P0: triple system S to the binary operation ⋆ where a ⋆ b = c iff {a, b, c} ∈ S or
L19@P0: a = b = c. In this paper we do not distinguish between these two concepts and
L20@P0: use them interchangeably.
L21@P0: A pasch configuration (or quadrilateral) in P3(X) is a set of four blocks
L22@P0: {a, b, c}, {a, d, e}, {f, b, d}, {f, c, e}
L23@P0: such that all elements a, b, c, d, e, f are distinct. An ST S(n) which does not
L24@P0: contain a pasch configuration is called anti-pasch (or quadrilateral-free). It
L25@P0: has been proved that for every admissible number n 6= 7, 13 there exists an
L26@P0: anti-pasch ST S(n), see [3].
L27@P0: The pasch configuration can be used to define an invariant of Steiner triple
L28@P0: systems, namely the number of pasch configurations contained in them. So
L29@P0: the class of anti-pasch Steiner triple systems is exactly the class for which this
L30@P0: invariant is zero. One can in fact use the pasch configuration to define more
L31@P0: invariants for Steiner triple systems which is the main focus of this paper.
L32@P0: ∗E-mail: aryapoor2002@yahoo.com
L33@P0-1: 12 Two invariants for Steiner triple systems
L34@P1: One invariant of Steiner triple systems is the number of pasch configurations in
L35@P1: them, see [4] for instance. Anti-pasch Steiner triple systems are those for which
L36@P1: this number is zero. So we need other invariants to study anti-pasch Steiner
L37@P1: triple systems. For example one can look for pasch configurations which have
L38@P1: exactly three blocks in a given STS. This idea is elaborated in what follows.
L39@P1: 2.1 Invariants and their properties
L40@P1: Suppose that S is an ST S(n). Associated to S, the sets A(S) and B(S) are
L41@P1: defined as follows. The set A(S) consists of all blocks B for which S ∪ {B}
L42@P1: contains a pasch configuration whose set of blocks contains B. In terms of the
L43@P1: associated quasigroup structure, it is easy to see that, we have
L44@P1: A(S) = {{a ⋆ b, b ⋆ c, c ⋆ a}|a, b, c ∈ Xare distinct and {a, b, c} ∈/ S}.
L45@P1: Inspired by this presentation, we set
L46@P1: B(S) = {{a ⋆ b, b ⋆ c, c ⋆ a}|a, b, c ∈ X are distinct}.
L47@P1: Note that {a⋆b, b ⋆c, c⋆a} = {a, b, c} iff {a, b, c} ∈ S. So we always have B(S) =
L48@P1: A(S)∪S. Set α(S) and β(S) to be the cardinals of A(S) and B(S) respectively.
L49@P1: To save space, set γ(S) = β(S)−α(S). These numbers are interesting invariants
L50@P1: of an ST S(n).
L51@P1: In order to study these invariants, it is useful to define the following maps

L56@P1: ψS({a, b, c}) = {a ⋆ b, b ⋆ c, c ⋆ a}.

L59@P1: Moreover ψS({a, b, c}) = {a, b, c} iff {a, b, c} ∈ S.
